title: Maximum Number of Removal Queries That Can Be Processed I
statement:
You get an array `nums` and an array `queries`. Before anything else you may, at most once, replace `nums` with any subsequence of it (delete any elements you like and keep the rest in their order). Then the queries are handled one by one in the given order. For `queries[i]`:

- if `nums` is empty, or its first element and its last element are both smaller than `queries[i]`, processing stops and no further query is handled;
- otherwise remove either the first or the last element of `nums`, choosing one whose value is at least `queries[i]`, and go on to the next query.

Return the largest number of queries that can be processed when the subsequence and every removal are chosen as well as possible.
notes:
## Intuition

Deleting elements up front means the only thing that matters is which elements end up serving queries: any element that is never used can be deleted at the start. So think of the process as peeling `nums` from both ends, where each peeled element either serves the next query (if it is large enough) or is simply discarded. After some peeling, what is left is always a contiguous block `nums[left..right]`.

For a fixed block, having served more queries is never worse: whatever a smaller count could still achieve, the larger count can match by using the same later removals for the later queries. So it is enough to store, for every block, the most queries served before reaching it. That is interval DP over shrinking blocks. Trying every subsequence and every left/right choice instead would be exponential.

## Approach

1. `step(done, value)` returns `done + 1` if `value` can serve query `done`, and `done` otherwise (the element is discarded).
2. `dp[left][right]` is the most queries served while everything outside `left..right` was peeled. The whole array starts at 0.
3. Go through blocks from longest to shortest. A block is reached either by peeling `nums[left - 1]` from the block one longer on the left, or `nums[right + 1]` from the block one longer on the right; keep the better result.
4. Every process ends with one element left to decide on, so the answer is the best `step(dp[i][i], nums[i])`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, `queries = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]`. Peeling from the left, `1` serves query 1, so `dp[1][4] = 1`; then `2`, `3`, `4` serve queries 2, 3, 4, giving `dp[4][4] = 4`. The last element `5` is smaller than `6`, so `step(4, 5) = 4`. No other block does better, and `best = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each of the about n²/2 blocks is filled from two neighbours in O(1).
- Space: O(n²) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- Guard `done < queries.length`: once every query is served, there is no next query to compare with.
- Do not forget the final single element: `dp[i][i]` counts queries served before it, and it may still serve one more.
- Discarding an element is allowed only because of the up-front subsequence; it never advances the query index.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `step` | serves the next query with `value` if it is big enough |
| `dp[left][right]` | most queries served when `nums[left..right]` is still untouched |
| `length`, `left`, `right` | size and ends of the current block |
| `best` | the largest count over all final elements |

narration.3: Peeling value while done queries are served: it serves the next query if it is large enough, otherwise it is just discarded.
narration.4: dp[left][right] is the most queries served while nums[left..right] is still untouched; the whole array starts at 0.
narration.6: Visit blocks from longest to shortest, so the blocks they come from are already filled.
narration.7: Slide the block's left end across every valid start.
narration.8: The block's right end follows from its length.
narration.9: The block can be reached by peeling the element just left of it...
narration.10: ...so take the count of that longer block and try to serve the next query with nums[left - 1].
narration.12: It can also be reached by peeling the element just right of it...
narration.13: ...so try nums[right + 1] on the next query and keep the better of the two results.
narration.19: Every process ends with a single element left to decide on.
narration.20: Let that last element try to serve one more query and keep the best total.
narration.22: The largest number of queries any choice can process.
